This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $h_t(d)$ be minimal such that every graph $G$ with $h_t(d)$ edges and maximal degree $\leq d$ contains two edges whose shortest path between them has length $\geq t$.
Estimate $h_t(d)$.
#934: [Er88]
graph theory
A problem of Erdős and Nešetřil. Erdős [Er88] wrote 'This problem seems to be interesting only if there is a nice expression for $h_t(d)$.'
It is easy to see that $h_t(d)\leq 2d^t$ always and $h_1(d)=d+1$. 
Erdős and Nešetřil and Bermond, Bond, Paoli, and Peyrat [BBPP83] independently conjectured that $h_2(d) \leq \tfrac{5}{4}d^2+1$, with equality for even $d$ (see [149]). This was proved by Chung, Gyárfás, Tuza, and Trotter [CGTT90].
Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang [CCJK22] conjectured that\[h_3(d) \leq d^3-d^2+d+2,\]with equality if and only if $d=p^k+1$ for some prime power $p^k$, and proved that $h_3(3)=23$. They also conjecture that, for all $t\geq 3$, $h_t(d)\geq (1-o(1))d^t$ for infinitely many $d$ and $h_t(d)\leq (1+o(1))d^t$ for all $d$ (where the $o(1)$ term $\to 0$ as $d\to \infty$).
The same authors prove that, if $t$ is large, then there are infinitely many $d$ such that $h_t(d) \geq 0.629^td^t$, and that for all $t\geq 1$ we have\[h_t(d) \leq \tfrac{3}{2}d^t+1.\]
Additional thanks to: Ross Kang

 The exact value $h_3(4) = 71$, with a machine-checked proof.
Kumar, Mohar and Pragada (arXiv:2607.02698, Lemma 3.1) recently refuted the CCJK conjecture at $\Delta = 4$ by exhibiting the odd graph $O_4 = \mathrm{KG}(7,3)$ — 35 vertices, 4-regular, 70 edges, every two edges within distance 2 — giving $h_3(4) \ge 71$. The lower bound is theirs, not ours.
We prove the matching upper bound, so $h_3(4) = 71$ exactly. The proof: an elementary finite reduction confining any extremal configuration to at most 80 vertices in four breadth-first layers; a counting bound showing at most 79 edges are arithmetically available; and an exhaustive certified search over the 123 surviving layer profiles. All of it is formalised in Lean 4, sorry-free on exactly [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]: the reduction, the counting bound, the exhaustiveness of the case split, KMP's witness, and the completeness of the propositional encoding. The only input from outside the proof assistant is the unsatisfiability of 123 explicit CNF formulas, each certified by an LRAT refutation checked independently of the solver that produced it. The certificates regenerate byte-identically from the published sources.
KMP's example already shows the projective-plane construction behind the CCJK conjecture, extremal at $\Delta = 3$, is not extremal at $\Delta = 4$; what is new here is that 71 is the exact value. We make no claim about uniqueness of the extremal graph, and nothing here bears on the asymptotic question; this is one exact value at one $(t, d)$.
The paper and the complete verification chain (Lean sources, manifests pinning all 123 certificates, checker source, a ~20-minute full regeneration recipe) are at github.com/bitterlemma/erdos-934.
This contribution is from the Bitter Lemma project ([email protected] — monitored; artifact requests answered). The mathematics, code, formalisation and text were produced with Claude (Anthropic) under human direction and review; every externally checkable component was verified by a pass independent of the one that produced it.

 Three things on this page, in decreasing order of certainty.
The page renders CCJK's conjecture as "$h3(d) \le d^3 - d^2 + d + 2$, with equality if and only if $d = p^k + 1$". Their paper says plain "if": "Conjecture. $h3(\Delta) \le \Delta^3 - \Delta^2 + \Delta + 2$, with equality if $\Delta$ is one more than a prime power." (Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, de Joannis de Verclos, Kang, Maximising line subgraphs of diameter at most t; the version accepted to SIAM J. Discrete Math.)
The page states $h1(d) = d+1$ unqualified. This was raised on this thread on 24 March 2026 and conceded the next day — it holds for $d \ge 3$ and fails at $d = 2$ because of $K3$. It is still on the page.
The page presents two CCJK conjectures with no indication that either has been settled. Kumar, Mohar and Pragada, An improved bound for the strong clique index of graphs (arXiv:2607.02698), disprove the $h3$ one — their $h3(4) \ge 71 > 4^3 - 4^2 + 4 + 2 = 54$ — and their Theorem 1.11 ($\liminf h3(\Delta)/\Delta^3 \ge 253/225$) also contradicts the $ht(d) \le (1+o(1))d^t$ clause at $t = 3$. (This is also laid out in the working report at erdosproblemaday.com/report/934, 28 July 2026, which this comment follows on that point.) In the other direction, the lower clause $h_t(d) \ge (1-o(1))d^t$ for $t > 2$ is the subject of the partial proof claim filed on this problem on 29 July 2026. Neither outcome is mentioned on the page.
The problem itself ("estimate $h_t(d)$") is of course still open; the point is only that the two displayed conjectures are no longer open in the direction the page implies.

 It is indeed assumed $d$ is large/ at least 3, since the d=2 case is a trivial case, 
since the only connected graphs with $\Delta \le 2$ are paths and cycles, and thence $h_t(2)=2t+2.$
For $d \ge 3$, let G have at least $d+1$ edges, then all other $d$ edges are incident to $uv$ and thus $u$ or $v$.
They cannot all be adjacent to a fixed one.
Now any edge incident with $u$ has to be incident with any edge incident to $v$, thus all of them are of the form $uz, vz$ for the same vertex $z$, which cannot happen.

A partial proof 
claimed by Samuel Korsky (using GPT 5.6-Pro).
 Summary:
 Confirming (and strengthening) a conjecture of Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang, we show that for $t > 2$,\[
h_t(d) \ge (1 - o(1))d^t \qquad \text{as}\ d\rightarrow\infty
\]using a construction involving complete flags over $\mathbb F_q^t$ for a prime power $q \sim d^{1/(t - 1)}$, in place of the generalized polygon constructions for $t \in \{2, 3, 4, 6\}$ for which the lower bound was already known. The key is to split a complete flag into its odd- and even-rank subflags and use those subflags as vertices in a cleverly designed regular bipartite graph.
